In 2000, she established the Volant Charitable Trust, named after her mother[371] to address social deprivation in at-risk women, children and youth, and to fund research into Multiple Sclerosis (MS).[372][373] She advocates for better MS care, and said, "For me, being able to campaign and fund-raise for multiple sclerosis is the most personally meaningful thing to have come out of being famous."[374] She was appointed president of One Parent Families (now Gingerbread) in 2004,[375] after becoming its first ambassador in 2000.[371] She collaborated with Sarah Brown[376] on a book of children's stories to benefit One Parent Families.[371] Together with the member of the European Parliament, Emma Nicholson,[377] Rowling founded the charity now known as Lumos in 2005.[371] Rowling has committed to covering all the core costs of Lumos, so that all other donations go directly to the work.[378] Lumos has worked with orphanages in Ukraine, Romania, Haiti, and Colombia, and it had supported at least 280,000 children by 2025.[175] She has donated several hundred thousand pounds to help women lawyers flee from the Taliban's control, helping hundreds of Afghans escape.[379]
Rowling has made donations to support other medical causes. She named another institution after her mother in 2010, when she donated £10 million to found a multiple sclerosis research centre at the University of Edinburgh.[380] She gave an additional £15.3 million to the centre in 2019.[381] To support COVID-19 relief, she donated six-figure sums to both Khalsa Aid and the British Asian Trust from royalties from The Ickabog.[221]

Several publications in the Harry Potter universe have been sold for charitable purposes. Profits from Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them and Quidditch Through the Ages, both published in 2001, went to Comic Relief.[371] To support Children's Voice, later renamed Lumos, Rowling sold a deluxe copy of The Tales of Beedle the Bard at auction in 2007; Amazon's £1.95 million purchase set a record for a contemporary literary work and for children's literature.[382][383] Rowling published the book and, in 2013, donated the proceeds of nearly £19 million (then about $30 million) to Lumos.[384][385] Rowling and 12 other writers composed short pieces in 2008 to be sold to benefit Dyslexia Action and English PEN. Rowling's contribution was an 800-word Harry Potter prequel.[386][r] When the revelation that Rowling wrote The Cuckoo's Calling led to an increase in sales,[195] she donated the royalties to ABF The Soldiers' Charity (formerly the Army Benevolent Fund).[371][388]
Views
Rowling was actively engaged on the internet before author webpages were common,[389] and used Twitter to reach her Harry Potter fans and followers.[390][391][392] She often uses sarcasm in tweets about her political opinions, sometimes generating controversy.[354][393]
Politics  
Main article: Political views of J. K. Rowling  
See also: Politics of Harry Potter
In 2008, Rowling donated £1 million to the Labour Party, endorsed the Labour prime minister Gordon Brown over his Conservative challenger David Cameron, and commended Labour's policies on child poverty.[394] In June 2024, she wrote that she had a "poor opinion" of Keir Starmer and that it would be hard for her to vote for Labour due to their position on transgender rights, which she argues comes at the expense of women.[395]

In her "Single mother's manifesto" published in The Times in 2010, Rowling criticised the prime minister David Cameron's plan to offer married couples an annual tax credit. She thought that the proposal discriminated against single parents, whose interests the Conservative Party failed to consider.[396] Rowling opposed the 2014 Scottish independence referendum, and donated £1 million to the Better Together anti-independence campaign.[397] She campaigned for the UK to stay in the European Union in the 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum. She defined herself as an internationalist, "the mongrel product of this European continent",[29] and expressed concern that "racists and bigots" were directing parts of the Leave campaign.[398]
She opposed Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but refused to support a cultural boycott of Israel in 2015, believing that depriving Israel of shared culture would not dislodge him.[399] In 2015, Rowling joined 150 others in signing a letter published in The Guardian in favour of cultural engagement with Israel.[400]
Press
Rowling has a difficult relationship with the press and has tried to influence the type of coverage she receives.[401] She described herself in 2003 as "too thin-skinned".[402] As of 2011, she had taken more than 50 actions against the press.[403] Rowling dislikes the British tabloid the Daily Mail,[404] which she successfully sued in 2014 for libel about her time as a single mother.[405]
The Leveson Inquiry into the British press named Rowling as a "core participant" in 2011. She was one of many celebrities alleged to have been victims of phone hacking.[406] The following year she criticised Cameron's decision not to implement all the inquiry's recommendations and supported the Hacked Off campaign, pushing for stricter media reform.[407][408]
Transgender people  
Main article: Political views of J. K. Rowling § Transgender people

Rowling has been described as a gender-critical feminist or trans-exclusionary radical feminist.[409] She rejects what she calls "gender identity ideology" and argues that gender self-identification does not override sex in determining who is a woman.[410] She is opposed to legislation that would allow transgender people to legally self-identify their gender without first receiving a medical diagnosis.[411][412][413] She believes that women-only spaces should be defined by sex,[414][415][416] which would prevent trans women from entering them.[417] These views are often described as anti-trans or transphobic.[418][409][417] Studies estimate that her positions and public profile make her an influential figure in the acceptability of transphobic discourse in the United Kingdom.[419][420]
Rowling publicly supported transgender rights in a 2016 speech to PEN America, but she became concerned about proposals to simplify legal gender recognition and what she regarded as their potential consequences for women-only spaces, particularly in prisons and services for survivors of sexual violence. The case of Karen White, a transgender prisoner who sexually assaulted women while housed in a women's prison, became an important influence in strengthening her concerns.[421] She spoke out in 2019 by defending Maya Forstater,[422] whose employment contract was not renewed after she made a series of tweets questioning UK government plans to let people declare their own gender.[354][423] (The Employment Appeal Tribunal later found that Forstater had been discriminated against.)[424][s] Rowling wrote that transgender people should live in "peace and security" but said she opposed "forc[ing] women out of their jobs for stating that sex is real".[429] According to the Harry Potter scholar Lana Whited, in the next six months "Rowling herself fanned the flames as she became increasingly vocal".[430]

MIT's proximity[s] to Harvard University ("the other school up the river") has led to a substantial number of research collaborations such as the Harvard–MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology and the Broad Institute.[260] In addition, students at the two schools can cross-register for credits toward their own school's degrees without any additional fees.[260] A cross-registration program between MIT and Wellesley College has also existed since 1969, and in 2002 the Cambridge–MIT Institute launched an undergraduate exchange program between MIT and the University of Cambridge.[260] MIT also has a long-term partnership with Imperial College London, for both student exchanges and research collaboration.[261][262] More modest cross-registration programs have been established with Boston University, Brandeis University, Tufts University, Massachusetts College of Art, and the School of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.[260]
MIT maintains substantial research and faculty ties with independent research organizations in the Boston area, such as the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory, the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.[232] Ongoing international research and educational collaborations include the Amsterdam Institute for Advanced Metropolitan Solutions (AMS Institute),[263] Singapore-MIT Alliance, MIT-Politecnico di Milano,[260][264] MIT-Zaragoza International Logistics Program, and projects in other countries through the MIT International Science and Technology Initiatives (MISTI) program.[260][265]
The mass-market magazine Technology Review is published by MIT through a subsidiary company, as is a special edition that also serves as an alumni magazine.[266][267] The MIT Press is a major university press, publishing over 200 books and 30 journals annually, emphasizing science and technology as well as arts, architecture, new media, current events, and social issues.[268]

MIT Microphotonics Center and PhotonDelta founded the global roadmap for integrated photonics: Integrated Photonics Systems Roadmap – International (IPSR-I). The first edition has been published in 2020. The roadmap is an amalgamation of two previously independent roadmaps: the IPSR roadmap of MIT Microphotonics Center and AIM Photonics in the United States, and the WTMF (World Technology Mapping Forum) of PhotonDelta in Europe.[269] In 2022, Open Philanthropy donated $13,277,348 to MIT to study potential risks from AI.[270]
Libraries, collections, and museumsedit  
See also: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Libraries and Campus of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology § Artwork
The MIT library system consists of five subject libraries: Barker (Engineering), Dewey (Economics), Hayden (Humanities and Science), Lewis (Music), and Rotch (Arts and Architecture). There are also various specialized libraries and archives. The libraries contain more than 2.9 million printed volumes, 2.4 million microforms, 49,000 print or electronic journal subscriptions, and 670 reference databases. The past decade has seen a trend of increased focus on digital over print resources in the libraries.[271] Notable collections include the Lewis Music Library with an emphasis on 20th and 21st-century music and electronic music,[272] the List Visual Arts Center's rotating exhibitions of contemporary art,[273] and the Compton Gallery's cross-disciplinary exhibitions.[274] MIT allocates a percentage of the budget for all new construction and renovation to commission and support its extensive public art and outdoor sculpture collection.[275][276] For example, the display boats, known as the Hart Nautical Collection, are located on the second-floor hallways of Building 5 (part of the main Maclaurin Buildings) at MIT in Cambridge, MA. The collection features numerous ship models, marine art, and boat plans that are on permanent display for visitors.

The MIT Museum was founded in 1971 and collects, preserves, and exhibits artifacts significant to the culture and history of MIT. The museum now engages in significant educational outreach programs for the general public, including the annual Cambridge Science Festival, the first celebration of this kind in the United States. Since 2005, its official mission has been, "to engage the wider community with MIT's science, technology and other areas of scholarship in ways that will best serve the nation and the world in the 21st century".[277]
Researchedit
MIT is classified among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity";[190] research expenditures totaled $952 million in 2017.[278] The federal government was the largest source of sponsored research, with the Department of Health and Human Services granting $255.9 million, Department of Defense $97.5 million, Department of Energy $65.8 million, National Science Foundation $61.4 million, and NASA $27.4 million.[279] MIT employs approximately 1300 researchers in addition to faculty.[280] In 2011, MIT faculty and researchers disclosed 632 inventions, were issued 153 patents, earned $85.4 million in cash income, and received $69.6 million in royalties.[281] Through programs like the Deshpande Center, MIT faculty leverage their research and discoveries into multi-million-dollar commercial ventures.[282]
In electronics, magnetic-core memory, radar, single-electron transistors, and inertial guidance controls were invented or substantially developed by MIT researchers.[283][284] Harold Eugene Edgerton was a pioneer in high-speed photography and sonar.[285][286] Claude Shannon introduced Boolean logic to circuit design, providing foundations for digital systems.[287] In the domain of computer science, MIT faculty and researchers made fundamental contributions to cybernetics, artificial intelligence, computer languages, machine learning, robotics, and cryptography.[284][288] At least nine Turing Award laureates and seven recipients of the Draper Prize in engineering have been or are currently associated with MIT.[289][290]

Current and previous physics faculty have won eight Nobel Prizes,[291] four ICTP Dirac Medals,[292] and three Wolf Prizes predominantly for their contributions to subatomic and quantum theory.[293] Members of the chemistry department have been awarded three Nobel Prizes and one Wolf Prize for the discovery of novel syntheses and methods.[291] MIT biologists have been awarded six Nobel Prizes for their contributions to genetics, immunology, oncology, and molecular biology.[291] Professor Eric Lander was one of the principal leaders of the Human Genome Project.[294][295] Positronium atoms,[296] synthetic penicillin,[297] synthetic self-replicating molecules,[298] and the genetic bases for Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig's disease) and Huntington's disease were first discovered at MIT.[299] Jerome Lettvin transformed the study of cognitive science with his paper "What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain".[300] Researchers developed a system to convert MRI scans into 3D printed physical models.[301]
Beginning in 1980, Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) was designed and constructed by a team of scientists from California Institute of Technology, MIT, and industrial contractors, and funded by the National Science Foundation. It was designed to open the field of gravitational-wave astronomy through the detection of gravitational waves predicted by general relativity.[302] Gravitational waves were detected for the first time by the LIGO detector in 2015. For contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves, two Caltech physicists, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish, and MIT physicist Rainer Weiss won the Nobel Prize in physics in 2017.[303] Weiss, who is also an MIT graduate, designed the laser interferometric technique, which served as the essential blueprint for the LIGO.[304]

MIT faculty have served as the president's science adviser four times, beginning with the first appointment to the role: James Killian, then MIT's president, who advised Eisenhower from 1957 to 1959.[413] He was followed by the electrical engineer Jerome Wiesner under Kennedy (1961–1964),[414] the geophysicist Frank Press under Carter (1977–1981),[415] and the biologist Eric Lander under Biden (2021–2022).[416][w] Other faculty have led federal agencies or held cabinet posts, including Ernest Moniz as secretary of energy (2013–2017),[419] Hans Mark (1979–1981)[420] and Sheila Widnall (1993–1997)[421][422] as secretary of the Air Force, Marcia McNutt as president of the National Academy of Sciences (2016–2026),[423] and Xavier de Souza Briggs as associate director of the White House Office of Management and Budget.[424]
MIT is the second-largest employer in the city of Cambridge.[425] Based on feedback from employees, MIT was ranked No. 7 as a place to work, among US colleges and universities as of March 2013.[426] Surveys cited a "smart", "creative", "friendly" environment, noting that the work-life balance tilts towards a "strong work ethic" but complaining about "low pay" compared to an industry position.[427]
Notable alumniedit  
For a more comprehensive list, see List of Massachusetts Institute of Technology alumni and List of Nobel laureates affiliated with Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Many of MIT's over 120,000 alumni have achieved considerable success in scientific research, public service, education, and business. As of October 2020, 41 MIT alumni have won Nobel Prizes, 48 have been selected as Rhodes Scholars,[428] 61 have been selected as Marshall Scholars,[429] and 3 have been selected as Mitchell Scholars.[430]

Alumni in United States politics and public service include former chairman of the Federal Reserve Ben Bernanke, former MA-1 representative John Olver, former CA-13 representative Pete Stark, KY-4 representative Thomas Massie, California senator Alex Padilla, and former National Economic Council chairman Lawrence H. Summers.[431]
MIT alumni have founded or co-founded many notable companies, such as Intel, McDonnell Douglas, Texas Instruments, 3Com, Qualcomm, Bose, Raytheon, Apotex, Koch Industries, Rockwell International, Genentech, Dropbox, and Campbell Soup. According to the British newspaper The Guardian, "a survey of living MIT alumni found that they have formed 25,800 companies, employing more than three million people including about a quarter of the workforce of Silicon Valley. Those firms collectively generate global revenues of about $1.9 trillion (£1.2 trillion) a year". If the companies founded by MIT alumni were a country, they would have the 11th-highest GDP of any country in the world.[432][433][434]
More than one third of the United States' crewed spaceflights have included MIT-educated astronauts, a contribution exceeding that of any university excluding the United States service academies.[435] Of the 12 people who have set foot on the Moon as of 2019, four graduated from MIT (among them Apollo 11 Lunar Module Pilot Buzz Aldrin). Alumnus and former faculty member Qian Xuesen led the Chinese nuclear-weapons program and became instrumental in Chinese rocket-program.[436]

Noted alumni in other fields include health care policy analyst and journalist Avik Roy, children's book author Hugh Lofting,[437][438] sculptor Daniel Chester French, guitarist Tom Scholz of the band Boston, the British BBC and ITN correspondent and political advisor David Walter, The New York Times columnist and Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman, The Bell Curve author Charles Murray, and United States Supreme Court building architect Cass Gilbert.[439] Other distinguished alumni include economist Esther Duflo,[440][441] who received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2019 for her experimental approach to poverty alleviation; physicist Mildred Dresselhaus, a pioneer in carbon science and recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom[442][443]; and physicist and science policy leader Shirley Ann Jackson, former chair of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission and president of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.[444][445]

MIT's proximity[s] to Harvard University ("the other school up the river") has led to a substantial number of research collaborations such as the Harvard–MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology and the Broad Institute.[260] In addition, students at the two schools can cross-register for credits toward their own school's degrees without any additional fees.[260] A cross-registration program between MIT and Wellesley College has also existed since 1969, and in 2002 the Cambridge–MIT Institute launched an undergraduate exchange program between MIT and the University of Cambridge.[260] MIT also has a long-term partnership with Imperial College London, for both student exchanges and research collaboration.[261][262] More modest cross-registration programs have been established with Boston University, Brandeis University, Tufts University, Massachusetts College of Art, and the School of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.[260]
MIT maintains substantial research and faculty ties with independent research organizations in the Boston area, such as the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory, the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.[232] Ongoing international research and educational collaborations include the Amsterdam Institute for Advanced Metropolitan Solutions (AMS Institute),[263] Singapore-MIT Alliance, MIT-Politecnico di Milano,[260][264] MIT-Zaragoza International Logistics Program, and projects in other countries through the MIT International Science and Technology Initiatives (MISTI) program.[260][265]
The mass-market magazine Technology Review is published by MIT through a subsidiary company, as is a special edition that also serves as an alumni magazine.[266][267] The MIT Press is a major university press, publishing over 200 books and 30 journals annually, emphasizing science and technology as well as arts, architecture, new media, current events, and social issues.[268]

MIT Microphotonics Center and PhotonDelta founded the global roadmap for integrated photonics: Integrated Photonics Systems Roadmap – International (IPSR-I). The first edition has been published in 2020. The roadmap is an amalgamation of two previously independent roadmaps: the IPSR roadmap of MIT Microphotonics Center and AIM Photonics in the United States, and the WTMF (World Technology Mapping Forum) of PhotonDelta in Europe.[269] In 2022, Open Philanthropy donated $13,277,348 to MIT to study potential risks from AI.[270]
Libraries, collections, and museumsedit  
See also: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Libraries and Campus of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology § Artwork
The MIT library system consists of five subject libraries: Barker (Engineering), Dewey (Economics), Hayden (Humanities and Science), Lewis (Music), and Rotch (Arts and Architecture). There are also various specialized libraries and archives. The libraries contain more than 2.9 million printed volumes, 2.4 million microforms, 49,000 print or electronic journal subscriptions, and 670 reference databases. The past decade has seen a trend of increased focus on digital over print resources in the libraries.[271] Notable collections include the Lewis Music Library with an emphasis on 20th and 21st-century music and electronic music,[272] the List Visual Arts Center's rotating exhibitions of contemporary art,[273] and the Compton Gallery's cross-disciplinary exhibitions.[274] MIT allocates a percentage of the budget for all new construction and renovation to commission and support its extensive public art and outdoor sculpture collection.[275][276] For example, the display boats, known as the Hart Nautical Collection, are located on the second-floor hallways of Building 5 (part of the main Maclaurin Buildings) at MIT in Cambridge, MA. The collection features numerous ship models, marine art, and boat plans that are on permanent display for visitors.

The MIT Museum was founded in 1971 and collects, preserves, and exhibits artifacts significant to the culture and history of MIT. The museum now engages in significant educational outreach programs for the general public, including the annual Cambridge Science Festival, the first celebration of this kind in the United States. Since 2005, its official mission has been, "to engage the wider community with MIT's science, technology and other areas of scholarship in ways that will best serve the nation and the world in the 21st century".[277]
Researchedit
MIT is classified among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity";[190] research expenditures totaled $952 million in 2017.[278] The federal government was the largest source of sponsored research, with the Department of Health and Human Services granting $255.9 million, Department of Defense $97.5 million, Department of Energy $65.8 million, National Science Foundation $61.4 million, and NASA $27.4 million.[279] MIT employs approximately 1300 researchers in addition to faculty.[280] In 2011, MIT faculty and researchers disclosed 632 inventions, were issued 153 patents, earned $85.4 million in cash income, and received $69.6 million in royalties.[281] Through programs like the Deshpande Center, MIT faculty leverage their research and discoveries into multi-million-dollar commercial ventures.[282]
In electronics, magnetic-core memory, radar, single-electron transistors, and inertial guidance controls were invented or substantially developed by MIT researchers.[283][284] Harold Eugene Edgerton was a pioneer in high-speed photography and sonar.[285][286] Claude Shannon introduced Boolean logic to circuit design, providing foundations for digital systems.[287] In the domain of computer science, MIT faculty and researchers made fundamental contributions to cybernetics, artificial intelligence, computer languages, machine learning, robotics, and cryptography.[284][288] At least nine Turing Award laureates and seven recipients of the Draper Prize in engineering have been or are currently associated with MIT.[289][290]
texts.26:
Current and previous physics faculty have won eight Nobel Prizes,[291] four ICTP Dirac Medals,[292] and three Wolf Prizes predominantly for their contributions to subatomic and quantum theory.[293] Members of the chemistry department have been awarded three Nobel Prizes and one Wolf Prize for the discovery of novel syntheses and methods.[291] MIT biologists have been awarded six Nobel Prizes for their contributions to genetics, immunology, oncology, and molecular biology.[291] Professor Eric Lander was one of the principal leaders of the Human Genome Project.[294][295] Positronium atoms,[296] synthetic penicillin,[297] synthetic self-replicating molecules,[298] and the genetic bases for Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig's disease) and Huntington's disease were first discovered at MIT.[299] Jerome Lettvin transformed the study of cognitive science with his paper "What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain".[300] Researchers developed a system to convert MRI scans into 3D printed physical models.[301]
Beginning in 1980, Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) was designed and constructed by a team of scientists from California Institute of Technology, MIT, and industrial contractors, and funded by the National Science Foundation. It was designed to open the field of gravitational-wave astronomy through the detection of gravitational waves predicted by general relativity.[302] Gravitational waves were detected for the first time by the LIGO detector in 2015. For contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves, two Caltech physicists, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish, and MIT physicist Rainer Weiss won the Nobel Prize in physics in 2017.[303] Weiss, who is also an MIT graduate, designed the laser interferometric technique, which served as the essential blueprint for the LIGO.[304]

MIT faculty have served as the president's science adviser four times, beginning with the first appointment to the role: James Killian, then MIT's president, who advised Eisenhower from 1957 to 1959.[413] He was followed by the electrical engineer Jerome Wiesner under Kennedy (1961–1964),[414] the geophysicist Frank Press under Carter (1977–1981),[415] and the biologist Eric Lander under Biden (2021–2022).[416][w] Other faculty have led federal agencies or held cabinet posts, including Ernest Moniz as secretary of energy (2013–2017),[419] Hans Mark (1979–1981)[420] and Sheila Widnall (1993–1997)[421][422] as secretary of the Air Force, Marcia McNutt as president of the National Academy of Sciences (2016–2026),[423] and Xavier de Souza Briggs as associate director of the White House Office of Management and Budget.[424]
MIT is the second-largest employer in the city of Cambridge.[425] Based on feedback from employees, MIT was ranked No. 7 as a place to work, among US colleges and universities as of March 2013.[426] Surveys cited a "smart", "creative", "friendly" environment, noting that the work-life balance tilts towards a "strong work ethic" but complaining about "low pay" compared to an industry position.[427]
Notable alumniedit  
For a more comprehensive list, see List of Massachusetts Institute of Technology alumni and List of Nobel laureates affiliated with Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Many of MIT's over 120,000 alumni have achieved considerable success in scientific research, public service, education, and business. As of October 2020, 41 MIT alumni have won Nobel Prizes, 48 have been selected as Rhodes Scholars,[428] 61 have been selected as Marshall Scholars,[429] and 3 have been selected as Mitchell Scholars.[430]
texts.39:
Alumni in United States politics and public service include former chairman of the Federal Reserve Ben Bernanke, former MA-1 representative John Olver, former CA-13 representative Pete Stark, KY-4 representative Thomas Massie, California senator Alex Padilla, and former National Economic Council chairman Lawrence H. Summers.[431]
MIT alumni have founded or co-founded many notable companies, such as Intel, McDonnell Douglas, Texas Instruments, 3Com, Qualcomm, Bose, Raytheon, Apotex, Koch Industries, Rockwell International, Genentech, Dropbox, and Campbell Soup. According to the British newspaper The Guardian, "a survey of living MIT alumni found that they have formed 25,800 companies, employing more than three million people including about a quarter of the workforce of Silicon Valley. Those firms collectively generate global revenues of about $1.9 trillion (£1.2 trillion) a year". If the companies founded by MIT alumni were a country, they would have the 11th-highest GDP of any country in the world.[432][433][434]
More than one third of the United States' crewed spaceflights have included MIT-educated astronauts, a contribution exceeding that of any university excluding the United States service academies.[435] Of the 12 people who have set foot on the Moon as of 2019, four graduated from MIT (among them Apollo 11 Lunar Module Pilot Buzz Aldrin). Alumnus and former faculty member Qian Xuesen led the Chinese nuclear-weapons program and became instrumental in Chinese rocket-program.[436]

**MacKenzie Scott** (née **Tuttle**, formerly **Bezos**; born April 7, 1970)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Statt-2) is an American novelist, philanthropist, and early contributor to Amazon. She was married to Jeff Bezos, the co-founder of Amazon, from 1993 to 2019.

As of December 2025, she had a net worth of US$40.0 billion, according to Bloomberg Billionaires Index, owning a 1.3 percent stake in Amazon.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-cbsdec2022-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-mks_net-5) As such, Scott was the third-wealthiest woman in the United States and the 40th-wealthiest person in the world.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-mks_net-5) Scott was named one of _Time_'s 100 most influential people in 2020 and one of the [world's 100 most powerful women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_list_of_The_World's_100_Most_Powerful_Women "Forbes list of The World's 100 Most Powerful Women") by _Forbes_ in 2021, 2023 and 2025.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-8)
In 2006, Scott won an American Book Award for her 2005 debut novel, _The Testing of Luther Albright._[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Wired-9) Her second novel, _Traps_, was published in 2013.

She has been executive director of Bystander Revolution, an anti-bullying organization, since she founded it in 2014.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-10) She is committed to giving at least half of her wealth to charity as a signatory to the Giving Pledge.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-11) Scott made $5.8 billion in charitable gifts in 2020, one of the largest annual distributions by a private individual to working charities.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-13) She donated a further $2.7 billion in 2021.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-14) As of December 2025, Scott had given a total of $26.3 billion to over 1,600 charitable organizations through her vehicle, Yield Giving.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-cbsdec2022-4)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Maruf-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-apscott24-16)

## Early life and education
[edit]
MacKenzie Scott Tuttle was born on April 7, 1970, in San Francisco, California, to Holiday Robin (née Cuming), a homemaker, and Jason Baker Tuttle, a financial planner.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Kulish-Ruiz-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Johnson-18) She has two brothers.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Kulish-Ruiz-17) She says she remembers writing seriously at the age of six, when she wrote _The Book Worm_, a 142-page book that was destroyed in a flood.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Bromwich-19)
In 1988, she graduated from the Hotchkiss School in Lakeville, Connecticut.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-20) In 1992, Tuttle earned her bachelor's degree in English from Princeton University, where she studied under Nobel Laureate in LiteratureToni Morrison, who in 2013 described her as "one of the best students I've ever had in my creative writing classes".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Bromwich-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Johnson-18)
After graduating from college, Tuttle worked as a research assistant to Toni Morrison for the 1992 novel _Jazz_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Bromwich-19) She also worked in New York City in an administrative role for hedge fund[D. E. Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._E._Shaw_&_Co. "D. E. Shaw & Co."), where she met Jeff Bezos.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Bromwich-19)

## Early life and education
Scott announced another $2.7 billion in giving to 286 organizations in June 2021.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-45)_Forbes_ reported that Scott donated $8.5 billion across 780 organizations in one year (July 2020 to July 2021).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-forbes2021-42) In February 2022, nine organizations announced gifts from Scott totaling $264.5 million.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-46) On March 23, 2022, more gifts were announced, including $436 million to Habitat for Humanity[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-47) and $275 million to Planned Parenthood.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-49) In May 2022, the Big Brothers, Big Sisters foundation reported a $122.6 million donation from Scott.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-50)
In April 2022, _The New York Times_ reported that Scott's donations since 2019 have exceeded $12 billion.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Kulish-Ruiz-17) As of November 2022, Scott had donated nearly $14 billion to approximately 1500 organizations,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Maruf-15) including Friends of the Children.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-51)

## Early life and education
In March 2023, Scott announced an "open call" for community-focused nonprofits with annual budgets between $1 and $5 million[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-apscott24-16) that she could fund.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-52) Lever for Change announced that Scott's open call for grants prompted 6,000 applicants.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-apscott24-16) The result was announced on March 19, 2024.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-cnn2024-53) She ended up donating $640 million to 361 small nonprofits, giving more than double what the original open call planned for,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-cnn2024-53) with 279 non-profits receiving $2 million each, and 82 groups receiving $1 million each.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-55)
By the end of 2025, Scott made a $45 million donation to The Trevor Project, having previously donated $6 million to the organization in 2020.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-56) In total, by the end of 2025, she had given away $26.3 billion.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-57)

Scott announced another $2.7 billion in giving to 286 organizations in June 2021.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-45)_Forbes_ reported that Scott donated $8.5 billion across 780 organizations in one year (July 2020 to July 2021).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-forbes2021-42) In February 2022, nine organizations announced gifts from Scott totaling $264.5 million.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-46) On March 23, 2022, more gifts were announced, including $436 million to Habitat for Humanity[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-47) and $275 million to Planned Parenthood.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-49) In May 2022, the Big Brothers, Big Sisters foundation reported a $122.6 million donation from Scott.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-50)
In April 2022, _The New York Times_ reported that Scott's donations since 2019 have exceeded $12 billion.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Kulish-Ruiz-17) As of November 2022, Scott had donated nearly $14 billion to approximately 1500 organizations,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-Maruf-15) including Friends of the Children.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-51)

In March 2023, Scott announced an "open call" for community-focused nonprofits with annual budgets between $1 and $5 million[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-apscott24-16) that she could fund.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-52) Lever for Change announced that Scott's open call for grants prompted 6,000 applicants.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-apscott24-16) The result was announced on March 19, 2024.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-cnn2024-53) She ended up donating $640 million to 361 small nonprofits, giving more than double what the original open call planned for,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-cnn2024-53) with 279 non-profits receiving $2 million each, and 82 groups receiving $1 million each.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-55)
By the end of 2025, Scott made a $45 million donation to The Trevor Project, having previously donated $6 million to the organization in 2020.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-56) In total, by the end of 2025, she had given away $26.3 billion.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacKenzie_Scott#cite_note-57)
